title: Resumo em português
text:
A pergunta. Um pet virtual dorme muito. Se o dono simulado fizer carinho logo depois de ele comer ou brincar, o pet fica mais acordado? O pet é guiado por um agente que aprende: quando recebe crédito de recompensa, a ação que acabou de fazer fica mais provável. Antes de rodar, a expectativa escrita era “não: dorme mais ou fica igual” (de uma olhada em 20 unidades de sementes de teste, fora dos dados da pesquisa).
O desenho, pré-registrado antes da rodada. 4 braços × 4 tipos de dono (atencioso, relapso, aleatório, incoerente) × 3 lugares da comida × 200 unidades pareadas (a mesma semente nos quatro braços) = 9.600 vidas de 14 dias simulados. Braços: sem carinho (controle); carinho só no corpo (sem crédito); carinho com crédito logo depois de comer/brincar; e o mesmo número de carinhos com crédito numa hora sorteada. Contrastes: D1 = com crédito − sem carinho (o efeito todo, primário); D2 = com crédito − hora sorteada (a hora); D3 = com crédito − só corpo (o crédito). Medida primária: a fração das decisões que não foram “dormir”; IC 95 % por t de Student sobre as 200 unidades. Cada vida tem 1.344 decisões (96 por dia, uma a cada 15 minutos simulados), e uma fração das decisões se lê como fração do dia. Tamanho relevante δ_A = 0,02 (cerca de 29 min do dia), sem fonte externa, escrito antes da rodada mas depois da olhada nas 20 unidades das sementes de teste (como a margem do tempo bem, 0,032). Regra de parada: rodar uma vez; custo projetado acima de 4 h → não roda.
O resultado oficial (cada número abaixo é recalculado do parquet e conferido com o resultado oficial, tolerância 1e-9):

L-ACORDADO: “não: com a recompensa o pet dorme mais”. D1 = -0,0109 [-0,0113; -0,0105], cerca de 16 minutos a menos acordado por dia simulado. O IC inteiro também cabe em ±0,02; a regra é lida em ordem e a primeira linha vale.
L-BEM: “o pet fica melhor”. D1 no tempo bem = +0,0183 [+0,0152; +0,0215]. Esse ganho não se separa do carinho no corpo: no tempo bem, o D2 é +0,0025 [-0,0007; +0,0056] e o D3 é +0,0012 [-0,0015; +0,0038], os dois IC incluem 0; os três braços com carinho ficam perto uns dos outros, acima do sem carinho. Não mostra que o crédito da recompensa faça bem ao pet. Por lugar (descritivo), o ganho está todo no lugar longe (+0,0598 [+0,0506; +0,0690]); nos outros dois o tempo bem cai, com o IC abaixo de 0, dentro da margem de 0,032.
L-PORQUÊ devolveu “pela recompensa na hora, e pelo que o pet aprende”, mas o rótulo foi escrito supondo que D1 teria o mesmo sinal de D2 e D3. Saiu o oposto: D1 -0,0109, D2 +0,0096, D3 +0,0070. O que os números mostram: o efeito do carinho no corpo faz o pet dormir mais; o crédito (D3) e a hora certa (D2) puxam de volta para acordado, sem cobrir a perda.

O bug e o conserto. Com as vidas já medidas e salvas, a análise parou com KeyError: 'saude_media': uma métrica de guarda pré-registrada (saúde nos dias 8–14) nunca foi gravada por vida, e o teste de fumaça não exercitava a análise. O conserto, commitado antes de ler qualquer número: a guarda saiu da lista e é relatada como NÃO MEDIDA; um modo de reanálise (--reanalisar) relê as medidas salvas e se recusa a rodar se o número de vidas ou de logs difere do plano. Nenhuma vida foi rodada de novo; nenhuma regra de leitura mudou.
Exploratório, depois do resultado. Só corpo − sem carinho: -0,0179 [-0,0183; -0,0175] (cerca de 26 min/dia), um contraste que não estava no plano. O modelo preditivo da página principal descreve esta simulação; não é causal e não substitui a leitura pré-registrada.
O que isto não mostra. Nada sobre jogadores reais (o dono simulado recompensa sempre e na hora); só uma dose de recompensa e nenhum outro tipo; só 14 dias e estas 12 células; nada sobre saúde (a guarda não foi medida); a separação entre crédito e corpo não é perfeita (os braços divergem depois do primeiro carinho, e o crédito alcança também os carinhos do próprio dono). Depois do resultado, a recomendação registrada foi não seguir com esta recompensa (nesta dose) como caminho para um pet mais acordado; outra dose ou recompensa seria uma pergunta nova, com plano próprio.
O que eu faria diferente. Testar a análise no teste de fumaça; escrever a regra do “porquê” para os dois sinais; justificar δ_A e as margens com uma fonte; planejar o contraste só corpo × controle; relatar efeitos absolutos e padronizados juntos.

title: Does reward keep a virtual pet awake?
text:
In short. A virtual pet sleeps a lot. I asked whether petting it right after it eats or plays (and giving its learning agent reward credit for that moment) would keep it awake more. Before running anything I wrote down the design, the outcome, the analysis and the rule that turns numbers into an answer. Then I ran it once: 9,600 simulated lives. The answer, read by the pre-written rule, was no: with the reward the pet sleeps more, slightly. Its welfare measure improved, but that gain cannot be told apart from what petting does to the body: it is not evidence that the reward credit itself makes the pet better off. The analysis crashed after the lives were saved; this page also shows that bug, how it was fixed before any result was read, and what I would do differently.
Every official number on this page is recomputed in a code cell from the published data (data/lives.parquet) and asserted against the official values (data/reference.json) to within 1e-9. Anything that was not part of the official, pre-registered result is marked Exploratory, after the result. Code is folded; click “Code” to see it.

title: Does reward keep a virtual pet awake?
text:
1. The question
The pet is a small simulated animal driven by a learning agent: when it receives reward credit, the action it just took becomes more likely. Its day is a long sequence of decisions (eat, play, sleep and so on), and in the simulation it sleeps a lot.
The question, in plain words: if its simulated owner pets it right after it eats or plays, does the pet stay awake more? Petting does two things at once: it changes the pet’s body state, and it can give the learning agent reward credit for what it just did. A careful answer has to separate those two.
Before the run I also wrote down what I expected: “no: it sleeps more or stays the same”. That expectation came from a quick look at 20 units run with the seeds reserved for the project’s software tests (“test seeds”), which are not part of the research data.

3. The design
Four arms (what happens around eating and playing) × four simulated owner types × three places of the food × 200 paired units. A unit uses the same random seed in all four arms, so every comparison between arms is a paired one. Each life lasts 14 simulated days.


Arms and contrasts

Owner types: attentive, neglectful, random, inconsistent. Places of the food: at_feeder, near, far. The 4 × 3 owner/place combinations are the 12 cells.
Primary outcome. awake_frac_d1_14: the fraction of the pet’s decisions over the 14 days that were not “sleep”. Each life has 1,344 decisions (96 a day, one every 15 simulated minutes), so a fraction of decisions reads directly as a fraction of the pet’s day. The project’s primary welfare measure, time_well (fraction of decisions taken while the pet was neither deprived nor exhausted), is read alongside it.
Analysis. For each unit, take the arm difference in each of the 12 cells and average them: one number per unit. The estimate is the mean of the 200 unit numbers; the 95% confidence interval is Student t over the units.
Relevant size. δ_A = 0.02 of the day awake. The plan marks it as having no external source: it is a judgement call, written down before the run but after the 20-unit look at test seeds mentioned above. The same holds for the welfare margin (0.032) and for the premise floors: the pre-registered minimums the design had to reach for a reading to hold (for example, at least 50 extra petting events per life in 95% of the lives). A premise that misses its floor is recorded and limits what can be read; it does not stop the run.

Applying the rules
The reading rules are code (in casestudy/__init__.py), applied to the recomputed intervals; the label they return is asserted against the label recorded in the official result.


Apply L-AWAKE, L-WELL and L-WHY

d2, d3 = res[("awake_frac_d1_14", "D2")], res[("awake_frac_d1_14", "D3")]
w2, w3 = res[("time_well", "D2")], res[("time_well", "D3")]

l_well = cs.read_well(w["ci_low"], w["ci_high"])
l_why = cs.read_why(l_awake, d2["ci_low"], d3["ci_low"], REF["dose_premise_held"])
for rule, label in (("L-AWAKE", l_awake), ("L-WELL", l_well), ("L-WHY", l_why)):
    assert label == REF["readings"][rule]["label"], (rule, label)
    CHECKS.append(f"reading {rule}")
within = -cs.DELTA_A <= a["ci_low"] and a["ci_high"] <= cs.DELTA_A
assert within
assert all(r["ci_low"] < 0 < r["ci_high"] for r in (w2, w3))  # the time-well caveat below relies on this
say(f"""
- **L-AWAKE: "{l_awake}".** D1 on the awake fraction is {cs.fmt(a)}: the whole interval is below zero.
  That is about **{abs(cs.minutes(a['mean'])):.0f} minutes less awake per simulated day**.
  The interval also fits inside ±δ_A, so the "stays the same" line would apply too; the rule is read
  in order and the first line ("upper < 0") applies.
- **L-WELL: "{l_well}".** D1 on time well is {cs.fmt(w)}: the lower bound is above zero.
  **This gain cannot be separated from the body effect of petting:** on time well, D2 is {cs.fmt(w2)} and
  D3 is {cs.fmt(w3)}, both intervals include zero. The three arms with petting sit close to each other,
  above no_petting, so the welfare gain is not shown to come from the reward credit or its timing.
- **L-WHY.** D2's lower bound ({d2['ci_low']:+.4f}) and D3's ({d3['ci_low']:+.4f}) are both above zero, so the

7. The bug and the fix
What happened. All lives had been simulated, measured and saved when the analysis stopped with
KeyError: 'saude_media'
One pre-registered guard metric (the pet’s health over days 8–14) had never been recorded per life. The smoke test before the run exercised the simulation but not the analysis step, so the missing field only showed up at the end.
The fix (committed 2 minutes after the lives were saved, before any result number was read):

The guard was removed from the list of measured outcomes and is reported as NOT MEASURED, rather than silently dropped.
A re-analysis mode (--reanalisar) reads the saved measurements and refuses to run if the number of lives or logs differs from the plan.
No life was re-run and no reading rule changed. Measuring the guard after the fact would have meant replaying the 9,600 logs (about 1 hour, estimated); it was not done.

8. Exploratory, after the result
Nothing in this section was in the plan. It does not change or replace the official readings above.

(a) The body effect alone: body_only − no_petting
L-WHY’s caveat says the body effect of petting pushes toward sleep. The plan had no contrast for that; here is its paired interval, computed the same way as D1–D3.


Paired CI for petting_body_only − no_petting
body = cs.summarize(cs.paired_differences("petting_body_only", "no_petting", "awake_frac_d1_14"))
arm_diff = REF["arm_means"]["petting_body_only"]["awake_frac_d1_14"] - REF["arm_means"]["no_petting"]["awake_frac_d1_14"]
assert abs(body["mean"] - arm_diff) <= cs.TOL  # balanced pairing: mean of differences = difference of means
say(f"**Exploratory, after the result.** petting_body_only − no_petting on the awake fraction: "
    f"**{cs.fmt(body)}** (about {abs(cs.minutes(body['mean'])):.0f} minutes less awake per day). "
    f"Petting that only acts on the body makes the pet sleep more, by more than the whole D1 "
    f"({a['mean']:+.4f}); the credit wins part of it back (D3 {d3['mean']:+.4f}). "
    "Caveat: arms diverge after the first petting, so this split between body and credit is not perfect.")


Exploratory, after the result. petting_body_only − no_petting on the awake fraction: -0.0179 [-0.0183; -0.0175] (about 26 minutes less awake per day). Petting that only acts on the body makes the pet sleep more, by more than the whole D1 (-0.0109); the credit wins part of it back (D3 +0.0070). Caveat: arms diverge after the first petting, so this split between body and credit is not perfect.




(b) A predictive model of the awake fraction
Exploratory, after the result. How much of the variation in the awake fraction across lives can be predicted from the design (arm, owner, place) and from what else happened in the life (eat and play decisions)? sleep_decisions is left out: it is the outcome itself. The petting count extra_pets is left out too: it is 0 only in no_petting and its level differs by arm, so it would carry the arm’s information and shuffling arm alone would understate how much the arm matters.

Cross-validation: GroupKFold with 5 folds, grouped by unit, so all 48 lives of a unit (4 arms × 12 cells) are held out together and paired seeds never leak between train and test.
Two models: a ridge regression (one-hot design + standardized counts, α chosen by internal CV) and a HistGradientBoostingRegressor (random_state=0).
Permutation importance on each held-out fold (R² drop, 5 repeats, random_state=0), with categorical variables permuted as whole columns.

This is a description of this simulation, not a causal analysis: eat and play counts are themselves consequences of the arm, and they are measured over the same days as the outcome.


GroupKFold CV, ridge and gradient boosting, permutation importance
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

CAT = ["arm", "owner", "place"]
NUM = ["eat_decisions", "play_decisions"]
X, y, groups = df[CAT + NUM], df["awake_frac_d1_14"].to_numpy(), df["unit"].to_numpy()
assert not {"sleep_decisions", "extra_pets"} & set(X.columns)

models = {
    "ridge": lambda: make_pipeline(
        ColumnTransformer([("cat", OneHotEncoder(), CAT), ("num", StandardScaler(), NUM)]),
        RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 13))),
    "gradient boosting": lambda: make_pipeline(
        ColumnTransformer([("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), CAT), ("num", "passthrough", NUM)]),
        HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0)),
}
scores, imps = {}, {}
for name, make in models.items():
    scores[name], imps[name] = [], []
    for train, test in GroupKFold(n_splits=5).split(X, y, groups):
        model = make().fit(X.iloc[train], y[train])
        scores[name].append(r2_score(y[test], model.predict(X.iloc[test])))
        pi = permutation_importance(model, X.iloc[test], y[test], n_repeats=5, random_state=0, scoring="r2")
        imps[name].append(pi.importances_mean)

How to read it. Where the food is and how often the pet chose to play explain the most variation between lives; the arm comes third, well ahead of eat decisions and owner type. The arm’s importance is not small, but it is not a measure of the effect’s size either: an R² drop says how reliably a column separates lives, and the paired design already showed that the arm difference is very consistent (large dz) while being only about 16 minutes a day. Play decisions are themselves partly a consequence of the arm, so the two share some of the same information. A high R² here says the simulation is fairly predictable from these columns. It does not say that changing any of them would cause the change, and it does not replace the pre-registered reading.

section: 9. What this does not show, and what I would do differently
text:
9. What this does not show, and what I would do differently
What this does not show.

Nothing about real players: the simulated owner rewards every time, and immediately.
Only one reward dose, and no other kinds of reward.
Only 14 days and these 12 cells.
Nothing about health: the guard was not measured.
Not that the reward credit improves welfare: the time-well gain is shared by all three petting arms.
The separation between credit and body effect is not perfect: the arms diverge after the first petting, and with owners that pet on their own, the credit also reaches the owner’s own petting.
δ_A, the welfare margin and the premise floors have no external source, and were written after the 20-unit look at test seeds.

After the result, the recommendation recorded was not to pursue this reward (at this dose) as the way to a more awake pet; another dose or reward would be a new question with its own plan.
What I would do differently.

Test the analysis in the smoke run, not only the simulation: run the full pipeline end to end on a handful of lives, so a missing field fails in minutes, not at the end of the whole run.
Write the “why” rule for both signs. L-WHY assumed D1 would move in the same direction as D2 and D3. A rule that names its sign assumptions would have produced a label that needs no caveat.
Justify δ_A and the margins with a source (a measured day-to-day variation, a design target or prior data) instead of a judgement call.
Plan the body-only vs control contrast. It turned out to be the key to interpreting the result, and here it can only be shown as exploratory.
Report absolute and standardized effects together from the start, so a large dz is never mistaken for a large effect.

title: Reproducing the official pre-registered results
text:
This notebook recomputes the official, pre-registered contrasts of the study from the published extract data/lives.parquet and compares them, number by number, with data/reference.json (the values computed in the original study). Nothing new is analysed here: the goal is to show that the published data reproduces the official numbers exactly.
The study in one paragraph. 9,600 simulated virtual-pet lives of 14 days each: 4 arms (what happens when the owner pets the pet right after it eats or plays) x 12 cells (4 owner types x 3 places) x 200 units. A unit is paired across arms: the same (unit, owner, place) appears once in every arm. See data/SCHEMA.md for the column dictionary.

title: Reproducing the official pre-registered results
text:
The three contrasts
Each contrast compares two arms, A minus B:

D1 = petting_with_credit - no_petting
D2 = petting_with_credit - petting_with_credit_random_time
D3 = petting_with_credit - petting_body_only

The six measures are: share of decisions that were awake over days 1-14 (awake_frac_d1_14, the primary outcome) and over days 8-14, the share of decisions taken while the pet was neither deprived nor exhausted (time_well), the share of hunger episodes closed by eating (episode_rate), and the number of eat and play decisions.

title: Reproducing the official pre-registered results
section: Step 1: one paired difference per unit (DuckDB)
text:
Step 1: one paired difference per unit (DuckDB)
For a contrast A - B and a measure, the official method works unit by unit. For each unit (1..200) and each of its 12 cells (owner, place) we take the measure in arm A minus the measure in arm B. Averaging these 12 differences gives one number per unit, so each contrast and measure ends up with 200 paired differences. The SQL below pivots the arms side by side per (unit, owner, place), subtracts, and averages over the 12 cells.


Code
con = duckdb.connect()

def paired_differences(a, b, measure):
    """200 per-unit differences (A - B), averaged over the 12 (owner, place) cells."""
    sql = f"""
        WITH wide AS (
            SELECT unit, owner, place,
                   max({measure}) FILTER (WHERE arm = '{a}') AS a,
                   max({measure}) FILTER (WHERE arm = '{b}') AS b
            FROM read_parquet('{LIVES}')
            GROUP BY unit, owner, place
        )
        SELECT unit, avg(a - b) AS diff
        FROM wide
        GROUP BY unit
        ORDER BY unit
    """
    return con.execute(sql).df()["diff"].to_numpy()

d = paired_differences("petting_with_credit", "no_petting", "awake_frac_d1_14")
print(len(d), "paired differences; first three:", d[:3].round(5))

title: Reproducing the official pre-registered results
section: Step 2: mean, 95% interval and effect size
text:
Step 2: mean, 95% interval and effect size
From the 200 differences we compute:

the estimate: their mean;
the 95% confidence interval: mean +/- t x sd / sqrt(200), with sd the sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) and t the exact Student-t quantile with 199 degrees of freedom (scipy.stats.t.ppf(0.975, 199));
the effect size dz: mean / sd of the same differences (reported for context; it is not in reference.json).



Code
rows = []
for cid, defn in CONTRASTS.items():
    for m in MEASURES:
        d = paired_differences(defn["a"], defn["b"], m)
        n = len(d)
        mean, sd = d.mean(), d.std(ddof=1)
        half = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 1) * sd / np.sqrt(n)
        r = ref["contrasts"][m][cid]
        rows.append(dict(
            contrast=cid, measure=m, n=n, estimate=mean,
            ci_low=mean - half, ci_high=mean + half, dz=mean / sd,
            diff_est=abs(mean - r["mean"]),
            diff_low=abs(mean - half - r["ci_low"]),
            diff_high=abs(mean + half - r["ci_high"]),
        ))
res = pd.DataFrame(rows)
res["max_abs_diff"] = res[["diff_est", "diff_low", "diff_high"]].max(axis=1)
res[["contrast", "measure", "estimate", "ci_low", "ci_high", "dz", "max_abs_diff"]].round(4)

Gate: the reproduction must match the official numbers
For every contrast x measure (18 rows), the estimate and both interval limits must be within 1e-9 of reference.json, and the four headline numbers must read exactly as above. If anything fails, this cell stops the notebook with an error; no tolerance or method is adjusted to make it pass.

title: Data dictionary: data/lives.parquet
text:
One row per simulated pet life: 9,600 rows, 13 columns. Each life lasts 14 simulated days and has 1,344 decisions (96 a day, one every 15 simulated minutes), so a fraction of decisions can be read as a fraction of the pet’s day.



Arms (4): what happens when the owner pets the pet right after it eats or plays.

no_petting (code R0): no extra petting.
petting_body_only (R-CORPO): extra petting acts on the pet’s body state only; the learning agent receives no reward credit for it.
petting_with_credit (R-CB): extra petting, and the learning agent receives reward credit for it.
petting_with_credit_random_time (R-SORT): the same reward credit, but delivered at a randomly drawn time instead of right after eating or playing.

Owners (4): attentive, neglectful, random, inconsistent (how reliably the simulated owner cares for the pet).
Places (3): at_feeder, near, far (where the pet’s area lies relative to the feeder).
Cells: 4 owners x 3 places = 12 cells.
Units: 200 per cell, numbered 1..200. A unit is paired across arms: the same (unit, owner, place) appears once in each of the 4 arms. 4 arms x 12 cells x 200 units = 9,600 lives.
